slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter four: the examination of the aggregates.

slides.heading: What is a cup made of?
points: A clay cup: solid, heavy, coloured
Form, explained by the four great elements
Is form found apart from its cause?
slides.say: Pick up a clay cup. It is solid, it has weight and colour, and it is made of something: clay, and the clay of earth and water. Buddhist schools called this physical side of things form, and they explained it by its causes, the four great elements. The fourth chapter asks a simple question about that explanation: can form be found apart from its cause, or its cause apart from form?

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: Chapter 3: the senses experience comes through
Chapter 4: what experience is made of
Form in detail; the other aggregates the same
slides.say: Chapter three examined the faculties that experience comes through. Chapter four examines what experience is made of: the five aggregates, the heaps into which the Abhidharma sorted everything about a person. It works through the first of them, form, in detail, and then says the rest go the same way.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
Nine verses
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: Five heaps
points: Form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness
No self apart from them: all schools agreed
Abhidharma: the heaps are real building blocks
slides.say: Now the explanation. The Buddha described a person as five heaps: form, which is the body and the physical world; feeling, pleasant, painful or neutral; perception, recognising this as that; formations, intentions and habits; and consciousness. No self is found apart from them. Every Buddhist school agreed on that. The Abhidharma went further. Having taken the self apart, it treated the aggregates, and the elements inside them, as real building blocks, each with its own nature. Form was said to be made of the four great elements: earth, which is solidity; water, cohesion; fire, heat; and air, motion. Chapter four tests whether this cause and made relation can hold between things that each have their own nature.

slides.heading: Form and its cause
slides.say: The first verse states the finding. Form is not found apart from its cause, and its cause is not found apart from form. If form existed apart from its cause, it would be uncaused. But nothing is uncaused; a cup does not appear from nowhere. If the cause existed apart from form, it would be a cause with no effect, and a cause with no effect is not a cause. Clay that never becomes anything is just clay, not the cause of the cup. This is chapter one, verse five, applied to matter: cause and effect are named together. So form and its cause are not two things, one sitting behind the other. They are designated in dependence on each other.

slides.heading: Before or after?
points: Form already exists: the cause has nothing to do
Form does not exist: nothing to be the cause of
Form with no cause: ruled out completely
slides.say: Verses four and five run the existence test. When the cause acts, either form already exists or it does not. If it already exists, a cause has nothing to do. If it does not exist, the cause has nothing to be the cause of. And form with no cause at all is ruled out completely. The conclusion: one should not build concepts around form. This does not mean we should stop thinking about tables. It means we should not build a theory in which form is a self-standing stuff, linked by a self-standing causal tie to self-standing elements. Each piece of such a theory fails when looked for.

slides.heading: Like or unlike?
slides.say: Verse four point six adds a test that recurs in later Madhyamaka. Is the effect like its cause or unlike it? If it were just like its cause, nothing new would have come about. If it were wholly unlike its cause, there would be no reason why this cause gives this effect: clay might as well give a song. The cup is neither the clay again nor unconnected to the clay. That middle position cannot be held by two things each with a fixed nature. It can be held by a relation in which both are named.

slides.heading: The same for every aggregate
slides.say: Verse seven extends the analysis. Feeling, mind, perception and formations, and indeed all things, go the same way as form. A feeling is not found apart from what it is a feeling of and the contact that gives rise to it. This is the turning point between early Buddhist analysis and Madhyamaka. Taking the person apart shows there is no self apart from the aggregates. But if the aggregates were kept as self-standing units, the self would be gone and a new set of substances would have taken its place. Nagarjuna takes the last step. The aggregates, too, are empty. The person is designated in dependence on the aggregates, and the aggregates are designated too.

slides.heading: Arguing with emptiness
points: A rebuttal assumes what is in question
The same analysis applies to it at once
No self-standing thing of one's own to defend
slides.say: The last two verses are a rule of debate. When someone argues by means of emptiness, any rebuttal stands in the same position as what is to be proved. Suppose an opponent replies: but the elements have their own nature, and they cause form. That reply simply assumes the elements are exactly the kind of thing whose existence is in question. The same analysis applies to them at once. In Chandrakirti's reading, the Madhyamaka does not have to defend some self-standing thing of its own. It is enough to show, on the opponent's own terms, that each proposed self-standing thing fails.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: Cups are still made of clay
Cause and effect: one relation, two sides
Nothing is a final building block
slides.say: Cups are still made of clay, and potters still need it. Physics still describes matter, and its descriptions still work. The chapter does not deny that form has causes. It denies that form and its causes are two self-standing things joined by a tie. Once that picture goes, cause and effect are seen as one relation named from two sides. The clay is the cause of the cup because the cup arises from it; the cup is made of clay because it arose from the clay. Nothing is a final building block, and nothing needs to be for the potter to work.

slides.heading: Check it now
points: Hold a cup
Where does the clay stop and the cup start?
It still holds the tea
slides.say: Hold a cup and look for where the clay stops and the cup starts. You will find the cup, and the clay, and no line between two separate things. The cup is not less real for that. It holds the tea.

slides.heading: In the books
points: Substrateless World: Introduction, Chapters 9 and 14
The Interlude, on conditions and causes
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World: the introduction, on the person designated on the aggregates; chapter nine, on Parfit and the middle way; chapter fourteen, on why convention is enough to function; and the Interlude, on conditions and causes. Links to all of them are on the chapter page. Next: chapter five, the examination of the elements.
